Based on the uploaded sources, here is a detailed synthesis of prior work on physics-based/hybrid baselines, smart meter analytics, the HEAPO dataset, the performance gap, and heat pump oversizing/cycling losses.

---

### 1. The HEAPO Dataset & Smart Meter Analytics

* **Dataset Overview & Metadata**:
  * **Source Title**: *2503.16993v1 (1).pdf* (HEAPO Preprint), Section 1 & Section 2.1.
  * **Scope**: HEAPO is an open-source dataset from ETH Zurich, EKZ, and the University of Bamberg containing smart electricity meter data (SMD) at 15-minute and daily resolutions from **1,408 real households** in the Canton of Zurich, Switzerland, recorded between November 3, 2018, and March 21, 2024 [1, 2].
  * **Record Length**: Households average **721.13 days** of daily data and **638.75 days** of 15-minute data [2].
  * **Cohorts**: Divided into **214 treatment households** (which have both SMD and on-site audit protocol data across 410 inspection reports conducted between 2015 and 2024) and **1,194 control households** (SMD only) [1-4].
  * **Population Statistics**: 55.26% use air-source HPs, 40.91% use ground-source HPs [5, 6]; 60.44% produce DHW via HP, 30.11% via electric water heater (EWH) [6, 7]; 24.36% own an EV, 36.65% have PV [6, 7]; mean heated living area is \\(193.28 \pm 71.65 \text{ m}^2\\), with \\(2.87 \pm 1.1\\) residents [6, 7].

* **Most Common Field Issues Identified in Protocol Reports**:
  * **Source Title**: *2503.16993v1 (1).pdf*, Section 3.3, Table 3.
  * Heating curve setting chosen too high: **40.98%** (168 visits) [8, 9].
  * Night setback mistakenly activated: **36.10%** (148 visits) [8, 9].
  * Heating limit setting chosen too high: **25.61%** (105 visits) [8, 9].
  * Descaling of DHW storage necessary: **17.80%** (73 visits) [8, 9].
  * Heat pump inappropriately sized / oversized: **10.00%** (41 visits) [8, 9].

* **Prior Smart Meter Analytics on this Cohort / Dataset**:
  * **Source Title**: *2503.16993v1 (1).pdf*, Section 1 & References.
  * **Load Disaggregation**: Brudermueller et al. [10] (BuildSys 2023) disaggregated heat pump load profiles from low-resolution smart meter data [11, 12].
  * **Inverter Identification**: Brudermueller et al. [13] (SmartGridComm 2022) differentiated variable-speed (modulating) from fixed-speed heat pumps using smart meter data [11, 14].
  * **Cycling Monitoring**: Brudermueller et al. [2] (Applied Energy 2023) monitored on-off cycling behavior across **503 Swiss households** using smart meter data [11, 14].
  * **Pre-selection & Intervention Savings**: Weigert et al. [15] (Energy Policy 2022) showed that pre-selecting inefficient heat pumps via smart meter data followed by on-site optimization reduced annual electricity draw by an average of **1,805 kWh (15.2%)** in half of the 297 inspected Swiss households [16, 17].

---

### 2. Physics-Based, Hybrid, and Residual Expected-Consumption Baselines & Fault Detection (FDD)

* **Degree-Day Change-Point Linear Regression (ASHRAE / NREL Protocol)**:
  * **Source Title**: *https://www1.eere.energy.gov/wip/pdfs/53827-8.pdf* (US DOE / NREL Chapter 8), Section 3.1 & Section 4.6.1.
  * Fits site-level 2-parameter (2P), 3-parameter (3P), or 4-parameter linear change-point models (PRISM) to separate weather-independent baseload (\\(\mu\\)) from temperature-sensitive heating (\\(\beta_H\\)) and cooling (\\(\beta_C\\)) slopes [137, 358, 376–378].
  * Variable degree-day base temperatures (\\(\tau_H \in 55^\circ\text{F}\text{--}70^\circ\text{F}\\)) optimize fit (\\(R^2\\), AIC, BIC) to capture building insulation, solar gains, and thermostat setpoints [380–384].

* **Short-Horizon Regularized ARX Model (FHNW Commissioning-Friendly FDD Tool)**:
  * **Source Title**: *https://irf.fhnw.ch/bitstreams/2f4c3f3c-65d8-4da5-aac5-af9cfaae720b/download* (Sawant et al., FHNW 2026), Abstract, Section 1 & Section 2.
  * Establishes a forecasting-based baseline using a Ridge-regularized ARX time-series model trained on as few as **3 fault-free reference days** immediately after commissioning [18-21].
  * Predicts 1-day-ahead supply flow temperature using 4 autoregressive lags (prev step, 1h, 1 day, 2 days), outdoor ambient temperature, and heat pump ON/OFF status [220–222].
  * Evaluates daily residuals across **3 complementary metrics**:
    1. *MaxAE* (Maximum Absolute Error) for short-lived spikes/transients [22].
    2. *RMSE* (Root Mean Squared Error) for global sustained offsets [226–227].
    3. *Pearson Correlation (\\(corr\\))* for diurnal pattern matching [227–228].
  * Combined via an OR-rule (\\(Fault = \text{RMSE} \ge T_{\text{RMSE}} \lor \text{MaxAE} \ge T_{\text{MaxAE}} \lor corr \le T_{\text{corr}}\\)) [23].
  * Tested on 12 real-world EoH monitored systems (capacities **4–16 kW**) + 1 synthetic dataset: achieved **0 false negatives (zero missed faults)** in 8 of 12 systems, with a mean false positive rate of **3.9 days per system** [182, 184, 230–231, 238–244].

* **Complementary FDD Methodologies in Sources**:
  * **ETH Zurich Component Diagnostics (Zogg 2002)**: Used dynamic grey-box models and steady-state physical models for component-level fault classification [197–198].
  * **DIBA-WP Project (HSLU)**: Catalogued **130 fault types** (investigating 27 in detail), identifying incorrect heating curves, source pump parameterization, auxiliary electric heating switchover, and defrosting degradation as top energy drivers [198–199].
  * **BEYOND Project (EIC Pathfinder 2024 / HPT Magazine 2025)**:
    * **Source Title**: *Soft Fault Diagnosis and Evaluation Strategies... HPT Magazine*, Sections 1–4.
    * Combines physics-based synthetic training data with Support Vector Machines (SVM) to evaluate concurrent soft faults, achieving an **82% balanced accuracy** in lab tests [155, 163–165].
  * **AI4HP Project (Fraunhofer ISE / BMBF 2024)**:
    * **Source Title**: *Artificial Intelligence for Heat Pumps - Fraunhofer ISE*.
    * Uses Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) and incremental learning for adaptive heating curve control, yielding **up to 10% energy savings** and a **50% reduction in comfort deviations** in practical tests [91–92].

---

### 3. Performance Gap & Prebound Effect

* **Performance Gap (Measured vs. Rated Performance)**:
  * **Source Title**: *2503.16993v1 (1).pdf*, Section 1. Nolting et al. [24] found real-world heat pump efficiency to be **up to 24% lower than rated values** [16, 25].
  * **Source Title**: *Soft Fault Diagnosis... HPT Magazine 2025*, Section 1. Hidden "soft faults" (refrigerant leakage, fouling, setting errors) increase daily energy consumption by **up to 26%** [155–156]. Undetected operational faults degrade overall system efficiency by **up to 25%** [26-28].
  * **Source Title**: *Wie gut sind aktuelle Wärmepumpen im Feld?* (OST WPZ Buchs / P+I 11/12-2020), Table 1. Real-world field JAZ in old buildings with high-temperature radiators (50–55 °C flow temp) drops to **2.8** (air-source) and **4.3** (ground-source), compared to **3.5** (air-source) and **4.9** (ground-source) in new builds with underfloor heating (30–35 °C flow temp) [29-31].

* **Prebound Effect**:
  * **not in the sources**. The specific term or concept of the "prebound effect" is not mentioned or evaluated in any of the uploaded documents.

---

### 4. Heat Pump Oversizing and Cycling Losses

* **Oversizing Prevalence & Economic Penalty**:
  * **Source Title**: *FAWA – Feldanalyse von Wärmepumpen-Anlagen* (BFE, 2004), Section 2.2 & Table 10.
  * Approximately **30% of heat pump installations operate at \\(\le 50\%\\) capacity utilization** under design outdoor temperatures (\\(T_{\text{design}} = -8^\circ\text{C}\\)) [307, 309–310].
  * Fleet-wide mean capacity utilization at design conditions is **70% (SD 0.22)** for air-source and **68% (SD 0.19)** for ground-source heat pumps due to installer safety margins ("better safe than sorry") [307–310].
  * Oversizing a heat pump by **35%** increases annual system costs by **8.3%** for air-source and **11.8%** for ground-source installations due to higher capital costs and oversized ground probes [32, 33].
  * **Source Title**: *protocols_variable_reference.md*, Section 6. In the HEAPO audit protocol dataset, out of 25 improperly planned installations, **19 were oversized** and **6 were undersized** [34]. Overall, improper sizing was flagged in **10.00%** (41 visits) of protocol reports [8, 9].

* **Cycling Losses & Hydraulic Buffer Sizing**:
  * **Source Title**: *Heat Pump Control Configuration: Heating Curve, SG Ready & DHW Settings* (iDM Energiesysteme, 2024), Sections "Why Control Configuration Is Needed" & "Buffer Tank".
  * Unconfigured controls cause overshooting and short cycling, increasing compressor starts, stressing components, and lowering COP [35-37].
  * Buffer storage tanks require a minimum volume of **\\(\ge 5 \text{ Litres per kW}\\) heat output** to ensure a minimum compressor run time of **10–15 minutes** and a minimum off time of **3–5 minutes** [36].
  * **Source Title**: *https://irf.fhnw.ch/bitstreams/2f4c3f3c-65d8-4da5-aac5-af9cfaae720b/download* (Sawant et al., FHNW 2026), Section "Data and Experimental Setup". Cycling faults caused by an oversized heat pump operating against insufficient buffer volume produce characteristic high-frequency supply flow temperature overshoots above the heating curve setpoint [38, 39].

---

💡 **Next Step**: Would you like to explore how any of these specific FDD algorithms or degree-day change-point models can be executed directly on the `smart_meter_data/` files in the HEAPO dataset using Python?

references.cited_text: Systems, University of Bamberg Bamberg, Germany thorsten.staake@uni-bamberg.de Abstract Heat pumps are essential for decarbonizing residential heating but consume substantial electrical energy, impacting operational costs and grid demand. Many systems run inefficiently due to planning flaws, operational faults, or misconfigurations. While optimizing performance requires skilled professionals, labor shortages hinder large-scale interventions. However, digital tools and improved data availability create new service opportunities for energy efficiency, predictive maintenance, and demand-side management. To support research and practical solutions, we present an open-source dataset of electricity consumption from 1,408 households with heat pumps and smart electricity meters in the canton of Zurich, Switzerland, recorded at 15-minute and daily resolutions between 2018-11-03 and 2024-03-21. The dataset includes household metadata, weather data from 8 stations, and ground truth data from 410 field visit protocols collected by energy consultants during system optimizations. Additionally, the dataset includes a Python-based data loader to facilitate seamless data processing and exploration.

To address these challenges, this work presents HEAPO (Heat Pump Optimization) – a real-world, open-source dataset designed to support researchers, practitioners, utilities, and other stakeholders in advancing both research and practical solutions for optimizing HP operations. For instance, HEAPO can be utilized to develop advanced algorithms, applications, and services for improving energy efficiency, disaggregating loads, leveraging flexibility in demand response programs, and estimating residential photovoltaic (PV) feedin to the grid. The dataset provides cleaned and ready-to-use energy data at both 15-minute and daily resolutions, recorded by standard smart electricity meters in 1,408 real households that use HPs for space and water heating. These households are located in the canton of Zurich, Switzerland. The field data was collected between 2018-11-03 and 2024-03-21, with each household having an average of 721.13 days of available data in daily resolution and 638.75 days in 15-minute resolution. Additionally, the dataset includes temperature data from the 8 nearest weather stations matched to household locations, metadata provided by households through an online tool from their utility company, and 410 field visit protocols recorded by professional energy consultants. These consultants, with over a decade of experience conducting energy audits, optimized the HPs during their on-site visits. For 214 of the households with available SMD, a corresponding audit protocol is available. Therefore, the protocols provide valuable insights into common issues observed in real-world installations and enable the analysis of changes in electricity consumption following the optimization, offering a unique opportunity to evaluate the impact of targeted interventions. To drive research advancements and scale real-world services, which still remain rarely deployed, high-quality data must be freely available to capture the variability of real-world system performance [21, 22, 35]. Understanding the factors that influence HP behavior and performance, as well as training algorithms to capture diverse usage patterns, requires a dataset that combines operational data with contextual information about the building and heating system, along with reliable ground-truth data on HP settings and optimization potential. There are several open-source datasets related to residential electricity consumption and HP usage, but none provide all the functionalities required for developing algorithms tailored to the aforementioned purposes [1, 27, 41, 42, 45, 46]. For instance, the dataset by Schlemminger et al. [46] offers residential electricity and HP load profiles from single-family homes in Northern Germany, recorded at resolutions ranging from 10 seconds to 60 minutes between 2018 and 2020. However, with data from only 38 households, the sample size is small, and the dataset includes very limited metadata on household characteristics, with no details on HP settings. Another well-known dataset in the HP domain isWhen2Heat by Ruhnau et al. [45], which provides synthetic national time series for heat demand and HP coefficient of performance across 16 European countries rather than real-world measurements. Other commonly used SMD datasets, often applied in non-intrusive load monitoring research, include REDD [28], UK-DALE [26], GREEND [36], and AMPds [34]. Among these, only AMPds contains HP measurements, providing one-minute power readings for a single house in Canada over two years. In summary, there is currently no publicly and freely available dataset with a large sample size that integrates SMD, metadata, and ground-truth data from residential buildings using HPs for heating or cooling.

Digital solutions for HP optimization are even more important in the light of a shortage of skilled workers. The European Union estimates a need for 750,000 additional installers, with at least 50% of the current workforce requiring reskilling [17]. In the UK, where HPs can only be installed by certified professionals, only 1,800 installers were certified in 2020, far below the 69,500 needed by 2035 [5]. This labor shortage affects both the deployment of new HPs and the optimization of existing systems. To address this, digital tools are essential for assessing system performance, identifying households with optimization potential, and prioritizing them for on-site interventions by professionals. While many modern HPs already transmit high-quality sensor data, including pressure, volume flow, and energy input/output, a significant number of existing units lack internet connectivity and advanced measurement capabilities [18, 24]. Yet, they will remain in operation for decades. In such cases, advanced metering infrastructure (AMI) with smart electricity meters (SMs) provides a scalable alternative for remote HP monitoring [6, 8, 37]. For example, a study using real-world smart meter data (SMD) from 503 Swiss households has already demonstrated that inefficient HPs can be identified by analyzing their on-off cycling behavior [7].
